Senses.Explanation: The opening turn of Linji's fourfold shine-work formula, posed, elaborated, recited, and oded upon across the corpus. Linji Yixuan's address to the assembly sets the four turns — sometimes shine first work later, sometimes work first shine later, sometimes both together, sometimes not together — with a person there in the first, a scheme there in the second, and in the third the ploughman's ox driven off and the starving man's food seized; Jingqing Daofu poses the four sayings himself and answers the first with clouds on the Nanyue ridge and a thief below the Taihang mountains; Langye Huijue elaborates the old one's formula in his own voice — shine first work later bares the lion's claws and fangs, work first shine later lets loose the elephant king's might, both together a dragon taking water, making rain and cloud; and Dahui Zonggao, citing the former sage, rules that the first blinds everyone's eyes, the second opens them, both together leaves them half-blind half-open, and not together wholly open and wholly blind. Tianyin Yuanxiu shames the fabricating elders who fix the shine before the work — have you even dreamed of my Linji's sweat? — reciting the whole formula he clearly tells you; Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen tells the assembly that after waking one must still pass through the ancestral schemes, reciting the four turns to school the thief-heart, warning the head-only walker he has feet and no eyes; Sanshan Denglai raises the root address, brushes it off with one 'not even needed,' answers his own asking with lighting the lamp and eating the rice, and opens his ode on the shine-first turn; and Eryin Mi, after raising the two opening lines, comments in matched verses — shine first work later, plainly one more awl behind the head — then outdoes them all: for the beyond-measure one everything shows whole at a touch, and what work would the shine still do?

Senses.Explanation: The second of the founding teacher's four illuminate-use gears — the blow that lands before the light, glossed from the source as the one where the way is in it. Linji Yixuan sets the fourfold out himself: sometimes illuminating first then using, sometimes using first then illuminating, sometimes both at once, sometimes not at once — the first has a person in it, the second has the way in it; Sanshan Denglai restates the whole set in his catechism and caps it with one pinch: no need of it; Tianyin Yuanxiu, attacking the fabricated elders who fix 'before' as light and 'after' as use, shouts the old master's own words back at them — did you ever dream of Linji's sweat? — he tells you plainly, sometimes using first then illuminating; and Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen, quoting the set, rules that today's people stop after awakening without piercing the compass or the great way — head-only men with feet missing, feet-only men with eyes missing. Dahui Zonggao, at the twin entombment, cites the old sages' four and extends them into eyes: if illuminating first, he blinds everyone's eyes; if using first then illuminating, he opens everyone's eyes; simultaneous, half-shut half-open; not simultaneous, all open all shut; Fenyang Shanzhao, preserved in Dahui's letter, welds the gear to the three mysteries — with use-first-then-illuminate, you too must be somebody; Eryin Mi appraises each gear in turn: first-illuminate adds an awl behind the skull, use-first demands re-examination under pressure, simultaneous — the pupil of the eye alive and quick, not-simultaneous — flowers in spring's season, fruit gathered after autumn; and Dabian Xianquan, setting the quote before his old-mirror verse, lets the ancient mirror stand on its stand with nothing held or released, the compass-pointer out and the wolf-smoke gone.

Senses.Explanation: In a finger snap measures an extremely short interval. Dahui Zonggao sets a hundred years against a finger-snap instant; Huiyue Xu says boundless affairs can be completed in that interval. Xuedou Chongxian uses the snap as a measure of immediate response, and Xuansha Shibei locates entry into Maitreya's tower within it.

Senses.Explanation: In a finger snap the eighty thousand gates are complete; in one leap enter the ground of the Tathagata. The paired line treats awakening as immediate rather than a sequence of measured steps. Current sources: Shiqi in J26nB183, Chushi Fanqi in X71n1420, Chunbei De in J38nB433, Tianru Weize in X70n1403. The complete saying and source turn control the sense. The many gates are figurative, not a numerical count.

Senses.Explanation: Out of compassion, a word spoken down in the weeds: Chan commentators use this saying when an older master chooses an accessible answer for a listener. Yuejiang Zhengyin says Wuzu's open-gate instruction was a compassionate accommodation, then contrasts it with his own response. Gulin Qingmao calls Yunmen's words to a monk a descent into accessible speech before showing his own whisk. Jie'an Jin says Manjushri's answer to a woman's question lowered the matter out of compassion, yet argues that answer alone did not free her. Sanshan Denglai labels Qingyuan's exchange a kindly descent into words in a case comment. Hanxiu Ruqian grants Weikuan's compassion but says his answer may leave hearers tangled in verbal explanations. Shanduo Zhenzai calls Longxing Zongjing's answer compassionate accommodation and offers a sharper reply of his own.

Senses.Explanation: To imitate the frown is to copy another person’s manner, with the famous beauty Xishi supplying the named original in one Zen reply. Yongjue Yuanxian says directly, “imitating the frown is not Xishi.” Other masters call their own verse or whisk demonstration the copied-frown expression, sometimes modestly and sometimes critically; the word therefore ranges from self-described imitation to a rebuke that the copy is not the original person.

Senses.Note: “When the hill across the valley nods” is an answer that places the next word behind an impossible sign. Dufeng immediately asks whether the hill has nodded yet. Yinyuan says it when asked what life a retreat protects, and Xueguan uses it rather than count hearers of a soundless lute. Baishan attaches the hill to a fuller reading of the dog Buddha-nature case. Jingting instead lets the hill nod in a sermon, showing the image can be revoiced rather than merely repeated.

Ying'an Tanhua, instructing the monk Zhan: under Mingguo's gate there is no Chan to speak, no way to transmit — one sword only; whoever comes, buddha or ancestor, saint or commoner, lift and cut; turn your body under that edge and you may leave one cloister for another and squeeze the old man on the seat — see the mouth still dripping, sling the satchel, walk: is it not a joy? Yuanwu Keqin, before the assembly: watch the ancients seal the news at an elder's word — Shuilao, taken by one of Mazu's treads, rose and roared laughing: a hundred thousand gates, an ocean of meanings, all recognized at the root of a single hair-tip — is it not a joy? and on to Linji's sixty blows and the rice-gruel plainness before Dayu. Senses.Explanation: The “spiritual light shines alone” evokes a clarity that needs no borrowed object or verbal support. Tianyin raises a whisk and brings the line into an address for the deceased, relating the light to the emptiness of wrongdoing. Feiyin says in a memorial verse that this light has not worn away over twenty years. Juelang writes a fresh verse linking the light with the simultaneous illumination of the senses. Yi’an describes a turn from muddied sensory experience toward this independent light. Wansong asks when one will know the light shining free of sensory entanglement as he comments on a case. Linquan uses the phrase in his own explanation of stillness and illumination. Faxi takes up the old formula before raising his whisk to give another answer. Jie’an brings the light into a New Year address, then asks for a word beyond old and new.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The luminous awareness shines by itself, entirely free of sense faculties and objects
AlternateTargets: Spiritual light shines alone, far beyond the sense roots and their objects
SearchAliases: free of sense roots and objects
Senses.Note: Baizhang’s line speaks of a clear light that does not depend on the split between the senses and what they encounter. Later masters reuse it in sermons, written guidance, and direct responses. “Light” is an image for what they ask a listener to recognize; it is not a claim about a visible lamp.

Senses.Explanation: The luminous awareness shines by itself, entirely free of sense faculties and objects states Baizhang’s image of clarity beyond the usual sensory split. Baizhang gives the line in his recorded hall teaching. Changming opens a sermon with it, then raises a whisk and points to the mountains behind the hall. Poshan sends it in direct guidance to a layman, urging him to see through the matter rather than wait for another explanation. Feiyin says such clarity appears when one no longer grasps or rejects. Faxi Yin gives the pair, raises a whisk, and asks the assembly whether they see and hear. Lüyan uses it while challenging an assembly to investigate beyond conceptual distinctions.

Senses.Note: The phrase names the Buddha's Vulture Peak gathering, conventionally associated with Kasyapa; present assemblies are compared with that inherited gathering.

Senses.Explanation: The Vulture Peak assembly names the Buddha's gathering conventionally associated with Kasyapa. Before the relevant question, Elder Lubei is twice met with a flick of the whisk when he is about to answer, followed by a hall address at the Ruzhou government office. The exchange asks what it is like when a human king meets the king of the teaching; the reply speaks of dancing around woods and streams without worldly sorrow or joy and, when asked what they discuss, of once sitting before Tiger-Leopard Cliff and spreading the true teaching in radiant light. The subsequent question says that Kasyapa personally heard the Vulture Peak assembly and asks how it should be proclaimed before the grand guardian that day. Thus the headword denotes the remembered Buddha assembly; the earlier exchanges establish the dialogue boundary, not another sense.

Senses.Explanation: The numinous or divining tortoise appears with shell, omens, diagram, book, and a tail that leaves traces. The most frequent Chan family is “the numinous tortoise drags its tail” (靈龜曳尾). The corpus explains the material action: on the ground it wipes its track, but the track arises again (拂迹迹生, “it brushes away the trace and the trace appears”). The Blue Cliff Record says that even someone with flashing responsiveness cannot avoid the tortoise dragging its tail. A later comment applies the same action to the Buddha holding up the flower and says traces are hard to remove. Asked for the Five Ranks, Boshan Suru Han answers that the numinous tortoise has no omen-lines and its empty shell need not be drilled. Other addresses have the tortoise enter the sea and swallow the moon, or pair the river-horse carrying a diagram with the tortoise bearing a book. The Zen-specific bend is the repeated use of this divining animal's tail, track, shell, omen, diagram, and burden as public comment, answer, and teaching-seat image; the entry does not convert those actions into a single abstract lesson.

Senses.Explanation: The numinous turtle drags its tail and thereby leaves the trace that betrays it. Chan masters use the image when an apparently quick, subtle, or traceless performance still exposes a residual mark by which it can be caught. Yuanwu says even lightning-fast eyes and function do not escape it; Tianran applies it to assertions of either mind and Way or no mind and no Way; Jianmen Nan says even perfect handling of the three seals leaves the tail; and Mingjue Cong calls an entry-answer the turtle’s self-made omen of ruin. Yuanwu also applies it to Xuedou’s added comment, and Dawei Jinglun uses it for Wuzu Fayan’s saying that cannot be retracted once heard.

Senses.PreferredTarget: The numinous turtle has no divination marks; there is no need to drill an empty shell
SearchAliases: the numinous turtle has no divination marks; there is no need to drill an empty shell
Senses.Note: After a monk asks whether a lotus is different before and after it rises from water, Hongzhi answers that the numinous turtle bears no divination marks and an empty shell needs no drilling. Linquan carries the image into another case about the intent of the ancestor, warning against forcing an omen from a question. Cian uses it in a verse about dropping borrowed supports and standing on one's own. Dachuan voices it after asking the assembly for yet another needle of explanation and strikes his staff. The image rejects the work of extracting a sign from what needs no extraction.
